newsitem.title: UK: New UK government vows smooth HK handover.
newsitem.headline: New UK government vows smooth HK handover.

text.p: Britain's new Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Monday that Hong Kong's smooth handover to China at the end of next month was one of the new Labour government's top priorities.
After telephoning Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten, Cook pledged his support for human rights in the colony that is returning to Beijing rule on June 30 after 156 years.
"The people of Hong Kong could be sure of a continued determination in London to make the transition successful," a foreign office spokesman said.
Cook, whose Labour Party swept to the biggest election victory in its history on May Day, pledged there would be continuity of policy after 18 years of Conservative rule.
Patten was reviled by Beijing for championing civil rights in the leadup to the handover.
The Foreign Office stressed after Cook's call to Patten: "The government is fully committed to the well-being of Hong Kong, in particular the rule of law and the rights and freedoms enjoyed there."

"A successful transition for Hong Kong on the basis of the Joint Declaration (the 1984 agreement between Beijing and London on sovereignty) is one of the government's top priorities," the spokesman said.
He said Patten, who has declined to enter the race for the Conservative leadership after John Major announced he is stepping down, is coming to London in the week of May 19 for talks with Cook.
Cook, in turn, would be flying to Hong Kong for the handover ceremonies.

Patten and the territory's future leader Tung Chee-hwa have congratulated Labour leader Tony Blair on his victory. Tung said he looked forward to working with Labour while Patten stressed the importance of bipartisan support for policies on Hong Kong.
Patten, the mastermind of John Major's victory in the 1992 British election, was playing tennis when he heard of Major's defeat on Friday. "Oh No!" Patten gasped.
But it was not clear if it was the poll results or his tennis game that upset him.
Patten has played down his ambitions, saying he needed a seat in the House of Commons before he could run for the top post in the badly divided and shell-shocked Conservative Party.

"I wouldn't advise anybody to put any money on me. One of the things which I lack in the party leadership stake is a seat in the Commons. I wouldn't take that seriously," he said after the election landslide for Labour.
